name: Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation
evidence_rating: thin: activity counts and stakeholder views; headline non-compliance indicator not tracked consistently; no independent studies found
summary: The CPC Regulation promised to cut widespread breaches of consumer law, which the Commission put at 37% of websites checked and about EUR 770 million in consumer losses in five online markets. Its 2024 review found joint actions against big traders work, but procedures are slow and national resources uneven, and recent checks still find more than a third of websites using manipulative designs. No study has measured whether consumer harm actually fell.

indicators.target_or_baseline: Baseline (IA): average 37% non-compliance in website screenings; detriment ~EUR 770m in five cross-border online markets
indicators.evidence: Sweeps keep finding high non-compliance (e.g. 2022 sweep: 37% of 399 websites used dark patterns); no consistent trend series against the baseline and no updated detriment estimate.

indicators.indicator: Mutual assistance requests where binding time limits were not respected
indicators.evidence: 2024 report describes coordinated-action procedures as 'long and cumbersome' but gives no systematic time-limit compliance figure in the sections reviewed.

indicators.indicator: Number of coordinated and common actions; number of alerts
indicators.evidence: Coordinated actions and alerts counted in the 2024 application report; alerts used unevenly across Member States; outcomes (commitments by major traders) reported qualitatively.

indicators.indicator: National enforcement plans; benchmarking of CPC resources
indicators.evidence: Report finds large differences in national resources are a main impediment; limited evidence on use of the new minimum investigation powers.

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws, SWD(2016) 164
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal for a Regulation on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws
literature.headline: Average non-compliance of 37% in website screenings; consumer detriment of about EUR 770m in five cross-border online sectors; reform expected to reduce non-compliance and detriment
literature.summary_plain: The Commission found more than a third of websites checked broke consumer law, costing consumers about EUR 770 million in five online markets, and expected stronger joint enforcement to cut this.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Report on the application of Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 on consumer protection cooperation, COM(2024) 311
literature.title: Report on the application of Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 on consumer protection cooperation
literature.method: application report (supporting study: surveys of authorities, alert entities and targeted traders)
literature.headline: Stakeholders consider objectives generally met and coordinated actions efficient; but procedures long and cumbersome, resources uneven across Member States, consumer groups say harm not significantly reduced; sweeps still find widespread non-compliance (37% of sites using dark patterns in 2022)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's review says joint enforcement against big traders works better than 27 separate actions, but procedures are slow, national resources uneven, and rule-breaking online remains widespread.

literature.authors: European Commission and national CPC authorities
literature.title: Sweeps (coordinated screening actions under the CPC Regulation), 2020-2025 results
literature.venue: European Commission, consumer protection enforcement web page
literature.method: coordinated compliance audits ('sweeps') of websites by CPC authorities: e.g. 223 review sites (2021), 399 web shops for dark patterns (2022), 16,000 products/176 sites on Black Friday (2022), 576 influencers (2023), 356 second-hand traders (2024), 314 traders on price practices (2025)
literature.outcomes: share of traders flagged as non-compliant with EU consumer law; cases earmarked for follow-up
literature.headline: Sweeps repeatedly find high non-compliance: 55% of review websites (2021), 37% of web shops using dark patterns (2022), 97% of influencers posting commercial content but only 20% disclosing it (2023), and only 40% of traders fully complying with price-reduction rules on Black Friday 2025.
literature.summary_plain: Under the cooperation regulation, consumer authorities across Europe check hundreds of websites at once for breaches. The checks keep finding that a large share of online traders break the rules, and flag them for follow-up.
literature.quality: Output and compliance monitoring of the CPC network, not an impact estimate; screening results before enforcement; Commission reporting on its own network
literature.interested_party: Commission coordinates the sweeps (reporting on its own network)
literature.citation: European Commission and national CPC authorities (2025), Sweeps (coordinated screening actions under the CPC Regulation), 2020-2025 results, European Commission, consumer protection enforcement web page

literature.authors: Bundesregierung (BMUV); external evaluation by AFC Public Services GmbH (O. Strecker, W. Voit)
literature.title: Bericht über die Anwendung des EU-Verbraucherschutzdurchführungsgesetzes durch Bundesbehörden (with AFC final evaluation report)
literature.method: external evaluation: case-statistics analysis of CPC requests 2007-2021, 31 stakeholder interviews, online survey and workshop
literature.outcomes: CPC information and enforcement requests, alerts, procedures and outcomes in Germany
literature.headline: Germany handled 382 CPC enforcement requests in 2007-2021 (about 25 a year); the evaluation finds the national CPC implementation effective, with early hearings by the Federal Environment Agency often ending infringements quickly.
literature.summary_plain: Germany's government had its handling of EU cross-border consumer enforcement evaluated and found the system works, with many cases settled quickly once companies are contacted.
literature.quality: Descriptive national evaluation spanning both the 2006 and 2017 CPC Regulations; ministry assessing its own law.
literature.interested_party: Ministry evaluating its own implementation (contracted external evaluator)
literature.citation: Bundesregierung (BMUV); external evaluation by AFC Public Services GmbH (O. Strecker, W. Voit) (2025), Bericht über die Anwendung des EU-Verbraucherschutzdurchführungsgesetzes durch Bundesbehörden (with AFC final evaluation report), Deutscher Bundestag Drucksache 20/14530, 8 January 2025

literature.title: An unfinished journey: Consumer groups' experience of CPC external alerts two years on
literature.method: case-based assessment of BEUC's four CPC external alerts filed since 2020
literature.outcomes: outcomes and procedure of external alerts under the CPC Regulation
literature.headline: BEUC used the new external-alert tool four times in two years; its airline alert led to commitments from 16 airlines, but transparency and speed of follow-up remain weak.
literature.summary_plain: The EU consumer federation reviews how the new right to alert enforcement authorities worked in practice: it brought results such as airline refund commitments, but slowly and opaquely.
literature.quality: Case evidence from the organisation's own alerts; self-interested assessment.
literature.interested_party: Campaigning consumer organisation; user of the mechanism it evaluates; EU co-funded
literature.citation: BEUC (The European Consumer Organisation) (2022), An unfinished journey: Consumer groups' experience of CPC external alerts two years on, BEUC report BEUC-X-2022-022
